name: Texas Method
author: Mark Rippetoe, Glenn Pendlay
structure: Three days built around one weekly record attempt. A volume day of 5x5, a recovery day of 2x5 at a light load, and an intensity day of one set of five at a new weight.
progression: The intensity-day set goes up about 2.5 kg (5 lb) a week and the other two days follow it. A stall is worked through in order: fewer volume sets, 5-10 % off the volume load, another rep scheme on the intensity day (2x3, 3x2, 5x1), then a week at half the intensity.
adapt: Put the three days in three routines. Written as a cycle, the volume and recovery loads are set from the intensity day's each week, as the method has it, and its stall sequence is applied when the log calls for it.
caveats: The volume day often runs past 90 minutes. Slow upper-body progress and little deadlifting.

name: Madcow 5x5
author: "Madcow", after Bill Starr
structure: Monday five ramping sets of five up to a top set; Wednesday four lighter sets; Friday four ramping sets, one set of three at a new weight and a back-off set of eight.
progression: Ramping sets step up about 12.5 % each. Starting loads are worked backwards so week four matches current bests and week five passes them; then squat goes up about 2.5 kg (5 lb) a week and bench and row half that. A missed top set repeats the week.
adapt: Its ramping sets step up at fixed intervals to a top set, and an exercise has one load for all its sets here. The weeks could be written out; the sets of one session cannot.
caveats: One of the most used bridges into intermediate training. The common advice to drop back about four weeks after a stall was not found in the source.

name: Bill Starr 5x5 (The Big Three)
author: Bill Starr, The Strongest Shall Survive (1976)
structure: Squat, bench press and power clean three days a week: a heavy day of five ramping sets of five to a top set, a light day at about 70-75 % and a medium day at about 80-85 %.
progression: The top set goes up the following week when it was completed.
adapt: Its ramping sets step up to a top set, and an exercise has one load for all its sets here. The weeks could be written out; the sets of one session cannot.
caveats: The origin of the modern 5x5 programmes. The power clean asks for technique. The original deload rules were not checked.

author: Jim Wendler
structure: One main lift a day in four-week cycles: a week of three sets of five, a week of threes, a week of 5/3/1, each with the last set open-ended, then a deload week. Every load is a percentage of a training max.
progression: The training max is 90 % of a one-rep max. Each cycle it goes up 2.5 kg (5 lb) for upper-body lifts and 5 kg (10 lb) for lower-body lifts, whatever the open sets did; a stall lowers it. The work sets are percentages of it: 65, 75 and 85 % for fives in the first week, 70, 80 and 90 % for threes in the second, 75, 85 and 95 % for five, three and one in the third, the last set of each open-ended. Those percentages were checked against the 5/3/1 for Beginners page, not against this entry's own source.
adapt: An exercise has one load a session here, so the three ascending sets cannot each have their own. The cycle carries the week's top set — its load, and its reps as the least to get — and the two lighter sets before it are the lifter's to do on the way up; say so in the summary. The weekly wave, the easier fourth week and the training max are written out in the cycle.
caveats: Sustainable and flexible. The original is low in volume and frequency, and monthly steps are slow for an early intermediate.

name: 5/3/1 Boring But Big
author: Jim Wendler
structure: The 5/3/1 main sets, then five sets of ten of the same lift or its opposite.
progression: As 5/3/1. The 5x10 load is 30 % of the training max in the first cycle, 45 % in the second and 60 % in the third, then stays at 50-60 % and rises with the training max.
adapt: An exercise has one load a session here, so the 5/3/1 top set is carried as in 5/3/1 itself, and the five sets of ten are planned on the opposite lift (its own exercise, its own load), not on the same lift again.
caveats: The most used 5/3/1 variant for size. Five sets of ten on the lower-body days is hard to recover from.

name: 5/3/1 First Set Last
author: Jim Wendler
structure: The 5/3/1 main sets, then the day's first-set load again for 3x5, 5x5 or one open set.
adapt: An exercise has one load a session here, so the first-set-last work cannot follow the top set on the same lift: the cycle carries the top set only.
caveats: Only its existence and outline are confirmed; no original text from the author was found.

name: 5/3/1 Building the Monolith
author: Jim Wendler
structure: Squat and overhead press on Monday and Friday, deadlift and bench press on Wednesday, in several sets of five with a top set at 85, 90 or 95 % of the training max by week; a 20-rep squat set on Fridays; a great many chin-ups, dips and face pulls every session.
progression: The training max is set at 85 % of the real max and adjusted in week four. No open sets and no deload week: a six-week push while gaining weight.
adapt: Needs the training max and weekly percentages of 5/3/1, which the app does not have.
caveats: Well regarded for gaining size; total volume and the eating it asks for are both very high.

name: 5/3/1 for Beginners
author: Jim Wendler; written up by the r/Fitness wiki
structure: Two main lifts a day (squat and bench, deadlift and overhead press, bench and squat), each for the three 5/3/1 sets and then 5x5 at the first-set load, with 50-100 reps each of a push, a pull and a single-leg or core accessory.
progression: The training max is 90 % of an estimated max and goes up 2.5 kg (5 lb) upper body and 5 kg (10 lb) lower body every three weeks. Week one is five reps at 65 and 75 % and five or more at 85 %; week two three reps at 70 and 80 % and three or more at 90 %; week three five at 75 %, three at 85 % and one or more at 95 %; each followed by 5x5 at the week's first-set percentage. A cycle that keeps missing its reps takes three steps off the training max.
adapt: Each main lift is done at three ascending loads and then for 5x5 at a fourth, and an exercise has one load a session here. The weeks themselves could be written out; the sets of one session cannot.
caveats: The programme the r/Fitness wiki sends people to after a novice routine.

name: nSuns 5/3/1 LP
author: u/nSuns (r/Fitness)
structure: Two programmed lifts a day, the first for many sets at changing percentages with a one-rep-or-more top set, plus accessories of the lifter's choosing.
progression: The training max starts at 90 % of a max and moves every week by the reps on the top set: none for 0-1, 2.5 kg (5 lb) for 2-3, up to 5 kg for 4-5, up to 7.5 kg beyond that. No deload is defined.
adapt: Every set is a percentage of a training max, and that max moves weekly from an open set. The app has neither.
caveats: Fast progress at very high volume and long sessions.

name: GZCL Jacked & Tan 2.0
author: Cody Lefever
structure: Three tiers. The main lift works up to a rep max each week and then does back-off sets; two second-tier lifts and accessories follow at falling intensity.
progression: Weeks 1-5 find a 10, 8, 6, 4 and 2-rep max; week 6 tests a single; weeks 7-11 take their back-off sets as a percentage of the week's rep max; week 12 tests again.
adapt: The rep target changes every week and the back-off loads are worked out from that week's top set. The app trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Builds strength and size together, with good reports. Not for someone who can still add load every session.

name: GZCL UHF (Ultra High Frequency)
author: Cody Lefever
structure: Close to full body on five days: an upper-body main lift is paired with a lower-body second lift and the other way round, and each day has its own percentages and reps.
progression: Percentages laid out in advance rise week by week, over five weeks or nine.
adapt: Loads are percentages laid out week by week; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Asks for a lot of judgement from the lifter. The stall rules were not checked.

name: GZCL The Rippler
author: Cody Lefever
structure: Upper/lower split. The main lift works from a two-rep max in sets of 1-5, the second lift from a five-rep max in sets of 3-6, and accessories take a fixed load for as many reps as it gives.
progression: The main lift moves in waves of 85 to 92.5 % of the two-rep max, up and back every two weeks; the second lift in three-week waves. Week 11 takes a heavy double and week 12 tests a single.
adapt: Loads are percentages of a rep max that wave up and down by week. The app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Written as the step after GZCLP.

name: GZCL General Gainz
author: Cody Lefever
structure: Each day one main lift worked in the 3-6 rep-max range and one second lift in the 6-10 range, each followed by shorter extension sets, plus two accessories.
progression: After finding a rep max the lifter chooses each session to hold it, add reps or add extension sets. The main lift goes up after a six-rep max with six extra singles; the second lift after a ten-rep max with all its half sets done.
adapt: The find, hold, push or extend choice is the lifter's own each session. The nearest thing the app runs is `double` over the same ranges (3-6 on the main lift, 6-10 on the second). Extension sets are not prescribed; they can be logged as extra sets.
caveats: Flexible and can run indefinitely. It needs honest judgement of how hard a set was.

name: SBS Strength — Reps To Failure
author: Greg Nuckols, Stronger By Science
structure: Sets at a percentage of a training max each week, with the last set taken to failure and compared against a rep target. Three seven-week blocks.
progression: Each rep over the target on the last set raises the training max by about 0.5 %; two or more under lowers it by about 1 % a rep. Weeks 7, 14 and 21 are deloads.
adapt: Built on a training max that is recalculated every week from an open set, with percentages that change through three blocks. The app has neither.
caveats: Its self-adjustment is well regarded. The spreadsheet is complex, the first block runs light and the third is tiring.

name: SBS Strength — RIR / Last Set RIR
author: Greg Nuckols
structure: Fixed load and reps a set, repeated until a set reaches the reps in reserve that were asked for; the number of sets completed is what is counted.
progression: More sets than the upper bound (six by default) raises the training max by about 2 %; fewer than the lower bound (four) lowers it by about 5 %. Weeks 7, 14 and 21 are deloads.
adapt: Built on a training max adjusted every week from how many sets were completed, with percentages that change through three blocks. The app has neither.
caveats: No weekly sets to failure, so fatigue is easier to manage than in the reps-to-failure version.

name: Greg Nuckols 28 Free Programs
author: Greg Nuckols
structure: Separate novice, intermediate and advanced templates for squat, bench press and deadlift, one to three days a week each, put together by the lifter.
progression: Percentages over four weeks, then a one-rep-max test that sets the next cycle.
adapt: Loads are percentages of a tested max that change week by week; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Easy to combine; accessories are left to the lifter.

name: Bullmastiff
author: Alexander Bromley, Base Strength
structure: One main lift a day with a developmental variation of the opposite pattern. A nine-week base phase in three waves (4x6, 5x5, 6x4 at rising percentages) and a nine-week peak phase of threes, twos and singles, with the last set of the week open-ended.
progression: A nine-week base phase in three three-week waves — 4x6 at 65 %, 5x5 at 70 %, 6x4 at 75 % of a max — and a nine-week peak phase at 80, 85 and 90 % for threes, twos and singles, the sets falling from five to three to one. The last set of each week is open-ended. Inside a wave, next week's load rises by 1 % of the max for each rep beyond the target on the open set, and stays when the target was only met. Each new wave starts again from its set percentage.
adapt: Written out as a cycle from its percentages. What a week's open set did is read after it is logged, and the next week's load moved by the programme's own rule then; the plan does not mark a set as open-ended, so say in the summary which set is.
caveats: The base phase is well regarded for size; opinions on the peak phase for a meet are mixed.

name: Barbell Medicine — The Bridge
author: Jordan Feigenbaum, Austin Baraki
structure: Three lifting days and one or two conditioning days. Four weeks of volume, the first of them easy and used to calibrate RPE; three weeks of intensity with reps falling from five to three; a last easy week.
progression: Every set is loaded to a target RPE, aiming for 2-5 % more at the same RPE each week. The last week drops to two or three sets a lift and keeps heavy singles.
adapt: Loads are chosen from an effort rating and the reps change by week. The app does not choose loads from RPE and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: A common first RPE programme; calibrating RPE takes practice.

name: Korte 3x3
author: Stephan Korte
structure: Squat, bench press and deadlift every session and nothing else: four weeks of high volume, then four weeks of heavy competition-style work.
progression: Percentages of a max laid out in advance, with a test at the end that sets the next cycle.
adapt: Loads are percentages laid out week by week across two phases; the app has no percentages and trains the same week until the plan is changed.
caveats: Very specific and very frequent. Only the outline was checked.
